summary: Defines a one-way metric for packet duplication, when more than one copy of a sent packet arrives. It complements the earlier packet loss metric, which counts when none arrive.

plainLanguage.summary:
When a packet is sent, normally exactly one copy arrives. Sometimes none arrives, and sometimes more than one does. The packet loss metric already covers the first case; this RFC covers the second.

The core measurement is simple: count the copies of one packet that turn up within a fixed waiting time. From that, the RFC derives a duplication count for a single packet and two percentages for a whole stream, one for how many extra packets arrived and one for how many packets were duplicated at all. The point is that two different measurement systems can report the same numbers and be compared.

questions: what is the one-way packet duplication metric
packet duplication fraction vs replicated packet rate
subtitle: A way to measure how often one packet arrives more than once, and how much of a stream that affects.

tldr.problem: A metric already existed for packets that never arrive, but nothing described the other failure mode: a packet that arrives two or three times, which can break receivers that expect exactly one copy.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a metric that counts how many copies of a packet arrive within a waiting window, a second metric equal to that count minus one, and two summary statistics over a stream of measurements.
tldr.outcome: Two measurement systems can now produce comparable duplication figures. The RFC was later updated by RFC 6248, which obsoleted the registry the metrics were registered in.

today: RFC 5560 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted. It was later updated by RFC 6248, which states that RFC 4148 and the IP Performance Metrics registry of metrics are obsolete.

sections.title: Why Duplication Needs a Metric
sections.content:
The document defines a metric for one-way packet duplication across Internet paths. It builds on the IP Performance Metrics framework of RFC 2330, and it follows the same structure as the document for one-way packet loss, RFC 2680.

The structure of the memo is layered. First, a singleton metric called Type-P-one-way-packet-arrival-count is introduced to measure the number of arriving packets for each packet sent. Then a second singleton metric, Type-P-one-way-packet-duplication, is defined to describe a single instance of packet duplication. That singleton metric is then used to define two samples, Type-P-one-way-Packet-Duplication-Poisson-Stream and Type-P-one-way-Packet-Duplication-Periodic-Stream, which measure duplication in a series of packets sent with either Poisson-distributed or periodic intervals between the packets. Finally, statistics that summarise the properties of these samples are introduced.

When a packet is sent from one host to another, one normally expects that exactly one copy arrives at the destination. It is, however, possible that a packet is either lost or that multiple copies arrive. The earlier packet loss metric distinguishes between cases where the packet arrives and where it does not arrive within a reasonable time. This memo defines a metric for a third outcome: a single packet is sent but multiple copies arrive. Since the document describes a case similar to the one in RFC 2680, all considerations from that document on timing and accuracy apply.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Although RFC 2119 was written with protocols in mind, the key words are used here for similar reasons: to ensure the results of measurements from two different implementations are comparable, and to note instances when an implementation could perturb the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC builds a measurement in layers, from one packet up to a whole stream, and then adds two summary percentages. The requirement words are used here to make sure two measurement systems produce results that can be compared.

sections.title: Type-P-one-way-packet-arrival-count
sections.content:
The metric takes the parameters src, the IP address of a host, dst, the IP address of a host, T, the wire time of a packet at the source, and T0, the maximum waiting time for a packet to arrive at the destination. Its unit is an integer number.

Two packets are considered identical if and only if both contain identical information fields, so the recipient could take either packet and use the data in an application while the other adds nothing, and both appear to have been sent by the same host to the same destination, hosts being identified by their IP addresses.

The value of a Type-P-one-way-packet-arrival-count is a positive integer giving the number of uncorrupted and identical copies received by dst in the interval [T, T+T0] for a packet sent by src at time T. If a packet is sent but is lost or does not arrive in that interval, the metric is undefined, and applications MAY report an impossible value such as -1 instead. If a packet is fragmented during transport and reassembly does not occur, the packet is deemed lost and is not included in the count.

The time-out value T0 SHOULD be set to a value at which the application could potentially still use the packet and would not discard it automatically. If this metric is used in parallel with the packet loss metric, the value of T0 MUST be the same in both cases so the results stay comparable. The metric counts only packets that were not corrupted during transmission, including packets that may have been resent automatically by lower layers or intermediate devices; packets that were corrupted but still arrived are not counted.

Clocks have to be synchronised between src and dst so that the interval [T, T+T0] can be determined accurately at both sides. If the metric is used in an active measurement system, the system MUST NOT send multiple packets with identical information fields, or all of them would be declared duplicates. The metric can also be used inside a passive measurement system with packets generated by another source, but if that source can send two identical packets within the interval, this will be incorrectly labelled as a duplicate, giving a false positive. It is up to the implementor to estimate whether that is likely and what rate of false positives is acceptable.

Identical does not necessarily mean that all bits in the packet are the same. When a packet is replicated and the copies travel along different paths, the Time to Live may differ. The implementation MUST specify which fields are compared. In IPv4 these will usually be version, ihl, identification, src, dst, protocol and some or all upper-layer protocol data; in IPv6, version, next header, source, destination and some or all upper-layer protocol data. The use of the identification field is not present in non-fragmented IPv6 packets and may not be sufficient to distinguish packets from each other even in IPv4, particularly at higher transmission speeds.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurement counts the copies of one packet that arrive within a set waiting time, treating copies as the same when they carry the same data and came from the same place. Copies damaged in transit do not count, and a packet that never gets through is reported as undefined rather than as zero.

sections.title: Type-P-one-way-packet-duplication
sections.content:
The second singleton metric, Type-P-one-way-packet-duplication, takes the same parameters, src, dst, T and T0, and its unit is also an integer number. Its value is a positive integer giving the number of uncorrupted and identical additional copies of an individual packet received by dst in the interval [T, T+T0], as sent by src at time T.

If a packet is sent and only one copy arrives in the interval, the metric is 0. If no copy arrives in the interval, the metric is undefined, and applications MAY report an impossible value such as -1 to indicate this condition.

The metric is equal to Type-P-one-way-packet-arrival-count minus 1. It is expected to be used by applications that need to know about duplication for an individual packet. All considerations regarding methodology, errors and reporting from the previous section apply.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the arrival count minus one. One copy means no duplication, three copies means two extra copies, and no copy at all means the figure is undefined.

sections.title: Samples for One-Way Duplication
sections.content:
Two samples are defined on top of the singleton metric, one for each way of sending packets.

Type-P-one-way-Packet-Duplication-Poisson-Stream takes the parameters src, dst, Ts and Tf, which specify the time interval when packets can be sent for this stream, T0, the maximum waiting time, and lambda, a rate in reciprocal seconds. Its unit is a sequence of pairs, each pair being a time T and the Type-P-one-way-packet-arrival-count for the packet sent at T. Given Ts, Tf and lambda, a pseudo-random Poisson process is computed beginning at or before Ts, with average rate lambda, and ending at or after Tf. The time values greater than or equal to Ts and less than or equal to Tf are selected, and at each of those times the value of the arrival count is obtained. The value of the sample is the sequence of the resulting time and duplication pairs. If there are no such pairs, the sequence is of length zero and the sample is said to be empty. Methodology, errors and uncertainties and reporting are as specified in the corresponding sections of RFC 2680.

Type-P-one-way-Packet-Duplication-Periodic-Stream takes the same parameters and has the same unit. At time Ts, packets are sent with a constant rate lambda until time Tf. For each packet sent the value of the arrival count is obtained, and the value of the sample is the sequence of the resulting time and duplication pairs. If there are no such pairs, the sequence is of length zero and the sample is empty. Methodology, errors and uncertainties and reporting are as specified in the corresponding sections of RFC 3432.
sections.plainLanguage: Both samples are just a list of pairs: the time a packet was sent, and how many copies turned up. One sample sends packets at random intervals, the other sends them at a steady rate.

sections.title: The Two Summary Statistics
sections.content:
The statistics in this section can be used for both the Poisson stream and the periodic stream, and the application SHOULD report which sample was used as input.

Type-P-one-way-packet-duplication-fraction gives the fraction of additional packets that arrived in a stream. Given a Poisson stream, one first removes all values of the duplication metric that are undefined. For the remaining pairs, one calculates the sum of the arrival counts divided by the number of pairs left, minus one. In other words, the number of packets received divided by the number of packets sent and not lost. The number can be expressed as a percentage. This statistic is the equivalent to the Y.1540 IPDR.

Type-P-one-way-replicated-packet-rate gives the fraction of packets that were duplicated, one or more times, in a stream. Again, undefined arrival counts are removed first. One then counts the number of pairs with an arrival count greater than 1, and calculates that count as a fraction of the total. In other words, the number of duplicated packets divided by the number of packets sent and not lost. The number can be expressed as a percentage, and the statistic is the equivalent of the Y.1540 RIPR.

The document works through four cases with a stream of four packets sent as 1, 2, 3, 4. In case 1 the packets arrive as 1, 2, 3, 4, so no packets are duplicated and both statistics are 0. In case 2 they arrive as 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, so every packet is duplicated once, the duplication fraction is 100% and the replicated packet rate is 100% too. In case 3 they arrive three times each, so the duplication fraction is 200% while the replicated packet rate is still 100%. In case 4 they arrive as 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, so half the packets are duplicated twice and the other half are not duplicated: the duplication fraction is again 100%, which does not show the difference with case 2, but the replicated packet rate is 50% here against 100% in case 2. The replicated packet rate will not show the difference between cases 2 and 3, so for that one has to look at the duplication fraction. Finally, the order in which the packets arrived does not affect the results, so permutations of case 2 yield the same values for both statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: Two percentages summarise a run of measurements. The duplication fraction says how many extra copies arrived in total. The replicated packet rate says how many packets were duplicated at all. A stream where every packet arrived three times and a stream where every packet arrived twice look the same on the second measure but not on the first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Conducting Internet measurements raises both security and privacy concerns. The memo does not specify an implementation of the metrics, so it does not directly affect the security of the Internet nor of applications that run on it, but implementations of these metrics must be mindful of security and privacy concerns.

There are two types of security concern: potential harm caused by the measurements, and potential harm to the measurements. The measurements could cause harm because they are active and inject packets into the network. The measurement parameters MUST be carefully selected so that the measurements inject trivial amounts of additional traffic into the networks they measure. If they inject too much traffic, they can skew the results of the measurement and, in extreme cases, cause congestion and denial of service.

The measurements themselves could be harmed by routers giving measurement traffic a different priority than normal traffic, or by an attacker injecting artificial measurement traffic. If routers can recognise measurement traffic and treat it separately, the measurements will not reflect actual user traffic. If an attacker injects artificial traffic that is accepted as legitimate, the loss rate will be artificially lowered. The measurement methodologies SHOULD therefore include appropriate techniques to reduce the probability that measurement traffic can be distinguished from normal traffic. Authentication techniques, such as digital signatures, may be used where appropriate to guard against injected traffic attacks. The privacy concerns of network measurement are limited by the active measurements described in the memo: unlike passive measurements, there can be no release of existing user data.
sections.plainLanguage: These measurements add traffic to the network, so they must add very little, or they distort what they measure. They can also be attacked: injected fake packets would make the numbers look better than they are.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has registered the metrics defined in the document in the IP Performance Metrics Metrics Registry, described in RFC 4148.
sections.plainLanguage: The metric names were entered in the IETF registry of IP performance metrics, so that measurement results can be labelled in a standard way.

viz.caption: THE FOUR EXAMPLES FROM RFC 5560, SECTION 5.3
WHAT COUNTS AS A COPY OF THE SAME PACKET

items.title: Same data
items.text: Both copies carry identical information fields, so either one would do for the application.

items.title: Same path endpoints
items.text: Both appear to come from the same source host and go to the same destination, judged by IP address.

items.title: Damaged copies do not count
items.text: A packet corrupted in transit is not counted, even if it still arrived.

items.title: A lost packet is not a duplicate
items.text: If a fragmented packet is never reassembled it counts as lost, not as a duplicate.

items.title: Clocks must agree
items.text: Both ends need synchronised clocks to fix the waiting window [T, T+T0].

viz.caption: THE TWO SUMMARY FORMULAS AS PRINTED IN RFC 5560

data.title: Summary statistics
data.code:
Type-P-one-way-packet-duplication-fraction
  = (Sum Type-P-one-way-packet-arrival-count / Number of pairs left) - 1
  = (number of packets received) / (number of packets sent and not lost)

Type-P-one-way-replicated-packet-rate
  = (number of duplicated packets) / (number of packets sent and not lost)
